outcome: every wake condition either resolves to met, unmet, an adapter error, permanently unsatisfiable (escalate), or explicitly unsupported — never silently stuck
notes: Precursor evidence for needs_input/waiting semantics (proposal §15.4).
rationale: A durable checkpoint (has this waiting Work's condition become true?) whose closed-set-of-outcomes semantics would survive reimplementation — matches §6.3.

statement: A wake condition's field names and value characters are both drawn from a strict allowlist — no field outside a fixed vocabulary is accepted, no value may begin with a dash (so it can never be misread as a flag by gh/td), and every field is additionally screened for secret-shaped names — before the condition is ever evaluated.
trigger: a wake condition file is read for evaluation
outcome: a wake condition can never smuggle an unexpected flag or a secret into a downstream gh/td invocation
rationale: Intake-hardening rule attached to the evaluate-condition checkpoint, not itself a checkpoint.

statement: A wake condition distinguishes 'unmet' (may still become true on a later attempt) from 'escalate' (has become permanently unsatisfiable, so continuing to retry would be dishonest and wasteful) — for example a GitHub check that has already concluded with a non-success outcome can never become success, so it escalates rather than being retried until the attempt budget or deadline runs out.
trigger: a wake condition is evaluated and found not yet satisfied
outcome: a permanently-unsatisfiable condition surfaces to the operator immediately rather than silently exhausting its retry budget first
rationale: A classification rule attached to the evaluate-condition checkpoint's outcome space.

statement: Retrying a not-yet-met wake condition uses exponential-feeling backoff with jitter recorded per attempt, and exceeding either a configured deadline or a configured maximum attempt count both terminate the waiting state — a deadline failure is terminal ('failed'), while exhausting max_attempts requires human input instead.
trigger: a wake condition remains unmet across repeated evaluations
outcome: a wait is always bounded: it either resolves, hard-fails at a deadline, or escalates to human input after too many attempts — never waits forever unbounded
notes: Direct engine-pressure evidence: this is precisely the durable, runtime-owned retry/backoff/deadline scheduling capability the current actor-stage-only engine does not yet have (captured as an engine-gap below).
rationale: §6.7's test — can the runtime, not the actor, own retry/backoff/deadline as a durable fact — applies directly: a durable wait with bounded, jittered retry and a hard deadline is exactly the class of ordering/retry state the proposal says the runtime, not an actor turn or an external cron script, must own.
alternatives_considered: An actor stage that itself sleeps and retries in a loop (rejected: burns a live model turn/token budget for the entire wait, and cannot survive a daemon restart mid-wait)

An externally cron-scheduled invocation of this same script (rejected: this is exactly today's mechanism — a helper script re-invoked by an external scheduler owns the durable backoff/deadline/attempt-count state as plain files, which is precisely the 'actor/external tool owns a durable fact instead of the runtime' anti-pattern §6.7 is testing for)

engine_gap.behavior: A Work waiting on an externally-observable condition (a CI check's conclusion, a sibling Work's completion, an external task tracker's status, an arbitrary future timestamp) must be resumed automatically once that condition becomes true, with bounded jittered retry between checks, a hard deadline after which the wait fails outright, and an attempt-count ceiling after which the wait instead escalates to human input — all without any actor consuming a live turn while merely waiting.
engine_gap.evidence: bin/sgt-wake plus its condition-file convention (.sergeant-wake-condition) implement exactly this today as a stateless script re-invoked by an external scheduler (cron/dagr), storing attempt count, last-attempt timestamp, and next-not-before entirely as plain files in fleet state.
lower_rungs_attempted: Represent waiting as an ordinary actor stage that polls in a loop (§6.4/§6.5)
Represent it as a helper invoked by an external scheduler, as today's mechanism does (§6.5/§6.6)
why_each_fails: An actor stage that polls in a loop either burns a real model turn indefinitely (wasteful, and incompatible with the per-turn-process execution model D2 measured and shipped) or exits after one check, at which point retry/backoff/deadline state has nowhere durable to live except back in the runtime.

A helper re-invoked by an external scheduler works only as long as something outside Sergeant (cron, dagr) keeps re-invoking it, and the retry/backoff/deadline bookkeeping is then owned by loose files rather than by the runtime's own event-sourced Work state, so it cannot be recovered, queried, or reasoned about the way every other execution fact in sergeant-rs is (journal-as-only-truth, CLAUDE.md).
engine_gap.minimum_capability_required: The runtime must be able to durably schedule a bounded, backoff-and-deadline-governed re-evaluation of an external condition for a specific Work, owning attempt count and next-eligible-time as journaled facts, and transition that Work automatically (met → resume, deadline exceeded → failed, max attempts → needs_input) without depending on an external scheduler to keep invoking anything.
engine_gap.acceptance_test: A Work is put into a waiting state with a github_check condition and a deadline; without any external cron job running, the daemon itself re-evaluates the condition on a bounded schedule, resumes the Work automatically the first time the check reports success, and if the deadline passes first, the Work is observed (via the API) to have failed with 'deadline exceeded' — all reconstructable from the journal alone.

statement: Evaluating an external GitHub check status always binds the query to the worker's own recorded worktree's remote, never to whatever repository the scheduler process happens to be running from, because the scheduler is normally invoked from somewhere other than the worker's own repository.
trigger: a github_check wake condition is evaluated
outcome: a resolution failure is never confused with a genuinely still-pending check
rationale: A binding-correctness rule for one specific adapter within the evaluate-condition checkpoint.

statement: A bounded, side-effect-free activity snapshot answers exactly one narrow question — is Sergeant verifiably doing work right now — as constant-size versioned JSON, and reports busy:true only when ALL of a stable in_progress status, an exact live worker pane identity match, and recent progress attributable to that exact pane hold together; every other outcome is busy:null, because absence of a verified witness is never treated as proof of idleness.
trigger: an external coordinator or bridge needs a side-effect-free, bounded answer to 'is Sergeant busy right now'
outcome: a caller can trust a busy:true result as verified evidence, and never mistakes an unverifiable observation for a confirmed idle state
notes: Directly maps onto the proposal's API/SSE + TUI/dashboard observation concerns even though today's mechanism is tmux/pane introspection (per source-inventory's own note on this file).
rationale: A meaningful, durable, three-valued checkpoint (true/null with a named basis) that any bridge or coordinator would want measured identically regardless of implementation — matches §6.3.

statement: The bounded activity snapshot is strictly read-only by design: it runs before any reconciliation, never writes anything, and deliberately avoids the pane-identity-migration side effect that the ordinary status-printing path performs, because a side-effect-free observation surface must never silently mutate state as a byproduct of being queried.
trigger: the bounded snapshot is being evaluated
outcome: querying activity status can never itself change durable state
rationale: A stage-independent rule (an observation surface must be pure) that would apply to any future read-only status endpoint, not one checkpoint's implementation detail.

statement: Fleet reconciliation recognizes a specific hazardous case — a status transitioning to done while the worktree's actual result file is empty — and refuses to accept it as a genuine completion, instead marking the Work orphaned with a diagnostic requiring a result before done can be trusted.
trigger: a worker's status reads done but its recorded result is empty
outcome: a claimed completion is never trusted without the substantive evidence (a non-empty result) that makes it genuinely terminal
rationale: A fail-closed validation rule attached to the sync-task checkpoint.

statement: Retiring a terminal (done, failed, or drained) worker's pane recycling evidence is bound to the exact pane identity being retired, not merely stamped as a permanent task-level marker — because binding to the wrong scope (any prior recycling ever) permanently suppressed recycling of every later relaunched pane once one pane had ever been recycled.
trigger: a terminal worker's pane needs to be recycled (its process resources reclaimed)
outcome: every distinct pane instance a Work ever used gets recycled exactly once, even across multiple relaunches of the same Work
rationale: A durable checkpoint (has this exact execution instance's resources been reclaimed?) whose per-instance, not per-Work, scoping would matter under any implementation — matches §6.3.

statement: Recycling a terminal worker's pane first settles its accepted notification action-lease before the pane is taken away, because recycling used to stop the only process that could ever publish completion, which is exactly how a completed turn became permanently unrecoverable.
trigger: a terminal worker's pane is about to be recycled
outcome: recycling never destroys the only process capable of proving a pending action was completed
rationale: An ordering rule attached to the recycle-terminal-worker checkpoint.

statement: Classifying a live in_progress worker as stalled treats tmux pane activity (any terminal output including tool calls and long-running commands) as the primary liveness evidence over a self-reported progress timestamp written by the worker's own supervisor loop, because a pgrep-based child-process check would incorrectly treat the supervisor's own delivery loop as meaningful activity.
trigger: an in_progress worker's liveness is being assessed
outcome: stall detection is never fooled by a supervisor process that is technically alive but doing nothing on the actual task
notes: D2-superseded pane-inspection mechanism, but the underlying lesson — a supervisor/wrapper process being alive is not evidence the wrapped work is progressing — is a durable design lesson for any future liveness signal.
rationale: tmux pane-output inspection is the exact interactive-pane mechanism D2 replaces with headless print-mode turns, where there is no persistent pane to inspect; the durable lesson (don't confuse a wrapper process's liveness with the wrapped work's progress) is worth preserving.

statement: A worker never launches with a harness it cannot honor: the capability gate (is the harness accepted), a readiness probe, and the launch invocation are all validated up front, before any fleet state directory is even created, so an invalid harness is rejected before durable state exists to clean up.
trigger: a worker supervisor is about to own an interactive harness pane
outcome: an unusable harness is rejected immediately, never discovered later as an unsatisfiable hang
rationale: A durable checkpoint (is this harness even usable?) that matters regardless of mechanism — matches §6.3.

statement: A worker resumed later by a response, a recovery, or a wake event always runs with the exact same pinned provider/model/variant tuple recorded at original dispatch time; a tuple the resuming harness cannot honor is a terminal failure, because silently falling back to the ambient default model is exactly the defect this contract exists to prevent.
trigger: a worker is launched or relaunched, whether at initial dispatch or on any later resume path
outcome: the exact model a Work runs on never silently drifts across a resume, and an unhonorable pin fails loudly rather than substituting
notes: Direct instance of the proposal's §6.1 example 'do not silently substitute a harness', extended to model pinning specifically; also directly evidenced by LESSONS L1's measured finding that model aliases silently substitute.
rationale: A broad, stage-independent rule (never silently substitute a pinned execution target) that applies to every launch and relaunch path uniformly, matching §6.1's own worked example almost verbatim.

statement: What a worker is about to run is recorded as durable, unfalsifiable launch evidence — harness, exact model, provenance of how the model was chosen, whether the provider/variant claim is independently verified by the launch mechanism itself or merely asserted — derived entirely from the validated tuple and the shared harness contract, never from the ambient environment, so the evidence can never carry a credential or an unverifiable claim.
trigger: a worker is about to launch its harness
outcome: every launch produces a durable, safe-to-read record of exactly what ran, distinguishing verified claims from unverified ones
notes: Direct precursor for the proposal's ExecutionRecord concept (§13.4/§16.4): distinguishing what is actually verified about a launch from what is merely asserted.
rationale: The launch_record shape (harness/model/model_source/provider_verified/variant_verified/...) is a durable evidence contract any execution-evidence consumer (an operator, a future audit, sgt-cleanup's evidence-preservation logic) reads the same way — matches §6.6.

statement: Launch evidence distinguishes intent from proof by a two-state field: it is written as 'intended' before the harness is even invoked, and only promoted to 'confirmed' once the harness is observably ready, so a harness that rejects the pin and exits immediately never leaves evidence claiming the model actually ran.
trigger: launch evidence is written both before and after the harness actually starts
outcome: launch evidence can never overclaim: an aborted launch is never mistaken for a confirmed run
rationale: A durable checkpoint (intended-vs-confirmed launch) whose evidence-integrity semantics matter under any mechanism — matches §6.3.

statement: A cooperative drain of one worker publishes every durable fact it can before terminating anything — a handoff, settlement of the outstanding action lease, and the drained status — and only after everything durable is published does it begin terminating processes, because a drain must never be a way to discard unfinished work.
trigger: an active global or project drain is detected while a worker is running
outcome: a drained worker's true, honest state (never a fabricated result) is fully durable before any process is terminated
rationale: A durable checkpoint (is the honest state published before anything is killed?) matching §6.3's stage test regardless of mechanism.

statement: Terminating a drained worker signals the whole process group, not just the worker's own shell, because a prior implementation signalled only its own subshell's BASHPID and left the agent, the notification loop, and the progress loop all running with the pane still open.
trigger: a drained worker's processes must actually be stopped
outcome: a drained worker's entire process tree is genuinely gone, not merely one shell within it
notes: tmux-pane/process-group signalling machinery obsolete under the daemon's own single-owner process-handle model (CLAUDE.md 'One owner') and D2's headless per-turn process lifecycle; the underlying lesson (terminate the whole tree, not just one shell) is durable.
rationale: Process-group signal escalation to terminate a tmux-pane-owned tree is exactly the machinery the daemon's exclusive process-handle ownership structurally replaces; there is no equivalent multi-process tree to terminate under a single headless `claude -p` turn.

statement: A worker's exit boundary settles the accepted notification action lease for every possible terminal status alike — done, failed, drained, needs_input, blocked, waiting, and orphaned — because every one of those exit paths is an equally valid place for a lease to be silently left outstanding forever if it is not settled at that single, unified boundary.
trigger: a worker process is exiting, regardless of outcome
outcome: a notification's action-lease fate is always known — finalized or explicitly pending with a reason — no matter which of the seven exit paths the worker took
rationale: Direct instance of CLAUDE.md's own named adjacent-append/exit-boundary hazard class (LESSONS L6): any path that can end a unit of durable work must be reviewed for exactly this class of gap. Matches §6.3's stage test as the single unified checkpoint every exit path funnels through.

statement: A worker's readiness gate for delivering a notification is bounded, not infinite: it waits at most a fixed timeout per notification target, and on timeout reports the unreachable state exactly once as durable, nonce-scoped evidence plus a recoverable needs_input gate — it never fabricates acknowledgement, acceptance, delivery, completion, or an action lease.
trigger: a harness never becomes ready to receive a notification
outcome: an unreachable harness always surfaces as an actionable, recoverable needs_input state, never a misleading terminal orphaned status and never an infinite hang
notes: Records a measured defect (unbounded spin previously reported misleadingly as orphaned) and the fix — a strong, evidence-backed durability rule.
rationale: A durable checkpoint (bounded readiness wait with an honest, once-only failure report) whose semantics matter under any mechanism — matches §6.3, and echoes the proposal's own timeout semantics (§15.6).

statement: A worker's exit is orphaned unless it produced a genuinely terminal status with substantiating evidence: a done status requires a non-empty result or the worker is reclassified orphaned; any other unrecognized status falls back to orphaned by default, so an unclassified exit is never mistaken for success.
trigger: a worker process is exiting
outcome: only a status with real substantiating evidence is ever accepted as a genuine terminal outcome; everything else defaults to the honest, investigable orphaned state
rationale: A fail-closed classification rule attached to the exit-boundary checkpoint.

statement: For the Claude harness specifically, whether a pinned model was actually honored — rather than silently substituted by the provider — is confirmed only after the run completes, by scanning the session transcript for a known substitution-warning phrase; this check never blocks or changes the mission's outcome, it only records a diagnostic that survives the otherwise-unconditional cleanup of that diagnostic on success.
trigger: a Claude worker with a pinned model has finished its run
outcome: a silent model substitution that a mission still completed 'successfully' is caught and durably recorded, even though nothing about the run's own exit signals failure
notes: Direct empirical confirmation of LESSONS L1's own finding ('model aliases silently substitute'), measured specifically against the real claude CLI, not assumed.
rationale: A verification detail attached to a post-run audit step, narrower than a full checkpoint since it never changes the mission's own terminal outcome — but load-bearing enough that it is not mere mechanics either; classified as stage-context under the launch/model-pin-fidelity invariant.

statement: A durable external callback event is delivered at-least-once but recorded exactly-once per idempotency key, is retried with exponential backoff bounded by a configurable cap, and every terminating callback response (ack, retry, reject) is validated against a strict schema before being trusted, so a malformed or oversized acknowledgement can never be mistaken for success.
trigger: a fleet task reaches needs_input, blocked, failed, or done, and an external callback origin is registered
outcome: an external system is durably, exactly-once notified of a fleet task's terminal or escalation events, with a documented retry/backoff contract and no ambiguity about what counts as acknowledged
notes: Precursor evidence for the proposal's Durable Callback Protocol (already captured under P1's docs/callbacks.md); this file is the mechanism half.
rationale: Bounded, independently invocable procedure (register origin → enqueue events → drain/retry until acked or sealed) with a clear completion condition (check-acked) — matches §6.2.

statement: Every callback profile executable must be verified, at the moment it is invoked, to be owned by the current user, not group/world writable, and executable by its owner — before it is ever run — so a callback profile can never be a trust boundary an unrelated user or process could tamper with.
scope: durable external callback delivery / trust boundary
trigger: a callback profile is about to be invoked
outcome: a callback can never execute an executable this process does not fully own and control
rationale: Deterministic, reusable ownership-verification machinery consulted by every callback-invoking path; not itself a checkpoint.

statement: A callback event's payload is rejected outright if it exceeds a fixed byte limit, contains more than sixteen lines, contains control characters other than tab/newline, contains command-metacharacters, looks like a shell command line, contains secret-shaped key=value pairs, or embeds a long numeric platform identifier — before it is ever queued for delivery.
scope: durable external callback delivery / payload safety
trigger: a callback event payload is being enqueued
outcome: an external callback can never receive a payload that looks like an injection attempt, a leaked secret, or an unbounded blob
rationale: Deterministic, reusable payload-hardening machinery applied uniformly at the enqueue checkpoint; not itself a checkpoint.

statement: A callback event's identity is derived by hashing its event type together with a caller-supplied source ID, and enqueuing the same (type, source) pair twice is idempotent — it returns the already-recorded event rather than creating a duplicate — so a caller can safely retry enqueuing without risking a duplicate delivery.
scope: durable external callback delivery / exactly-once semantics
trigger: a caller enqueues a callback event that may have already been enqueued
outcome: the same logical event is never recorded, or delivered, more than once, regardless of how many times the enqueuing caller retries
rationale: A durable checkpoint (is this event new or a retry of an existing one?) whose exactly-once semantics matter under any storage mechanism — matches §6.3.

statement: Draining pending callback events claims one event at a time under a lock (marking it 'delivering' with a claim timestamp before releasing the lock to actually invoke the external profile), and a claim that has sat unresolved past a claim timeout is treated as abandoned and reclaimable by a later drain pass, rather than staying stuck forever.
trigger: a callback drain pass is selecting the next event to attempt delivery for
outcome: a crashed or stuck delivery attempt is automatically reclaimed by a later drain pass instead of permanently blocking that event
rationale: A crash-recovery rule attached to the drain checkpoint's claim mechanism.

statement: A fleet task's callback events cannot be cleaned up (sealed) while any event for it remains unacknowledged, and once sealed a callback task's event history is marked retired rather than deleted, so no cleanup can silently discard an external system's undelivered or unacknowledged notification.
scope: durable external callback delivery / cleanup safety
trigger: fleet state cleanup wants to retire a task's callback history
outcome: cleanup can never destroy evidence of an external notification that has not been proven to have been received
rationale: A durable checkpoint (has every callback for this task actually been acknowledged before its evidence is retired?) that matters under any implementation — matches §6.3.

statement: Dispatch is a bounded, independently invocable procedure: given a project, a brief (or a tracked-work task reference), and a set of target repos, it produces one durable task with an isolated worktree, a rendered mission brief, and a spawned interactive worker per repo — with every side effect (tracked-work creation, worktree acquisition, pane launch) validated and gated before the next repo's dispatch begins.
trigger: an operator or an automated caller (dagr hook) needs a piece of work executed by an agent in one or more repos
outcome: a durable, observable Work exists per targeted repo, each with its own isolated code snapshot and a running worker
rationale: Recognizable trigger and bounded, independently invocable outcome (a Work exists and is running) — matches §6.2 directly, and is explicitly named as such in the proposal's §8.2 representative-procedures list.
alternatives_considered: obsolete-mechanism (rejected for the whole procedure: the durable procedure — resolve intent, validate targets, acquire isolated code, launch, verify — survives reimplementation even though tmux/worktree specifics do not)

statement: Which pinned model tuple a dispatched worker will run is resolved with a fixed, explicit-only precedence — a per-invocation flag beats an environment variable, which beats no pin at all — with no project-level or per-repo default in the precedence chain by deliberate decision, not by omission, and the resolution and its shape are both validated before any intent file, task, or worktree exists.
trigger: a dispatch is choosing which model tuple to pin for its workers
outcome: the source of a pinned model is always explicit and recorded, never an implicit config default a caller might not realize is in effect
rationale: A durable checkpoint (which tuple, and from which explicit source, was chosen) that matters under any implementation — matches §6.3.

statement: Dispatch refuses to re-dispatch onto a branch that already carries committed work unreachable from any remote, unless the operator explicitly opts in with an adopt-branch flag, because a prior interrupted dispatch may have done real, unpreserved work that a fresh dispatch would silently discard or duplicate.
trigger: dispatch is about to reuse an existing branch name
outcome: preserved but unpushed work from an interrupted prior dispatch is never silently lost or duplicated by a fresh dispatch
notes: Reachability is checked against ANY remote, not just origin, specifically because checking only origin previously blocked resuming preserved work in any repo the operator could not push to (regression fix, cites td-7f3a9a).
rationale: A durable checkpoint (does this branch carry unpreserved prior work?) whose safety property would matter under any mechanism — matches §6.3.

statement: Every repo's identity-switching, worktree acquisition, brief writing, and worker launch is validated in order such that any failure records an orphaned status with a specific diagnostic and a handoff before the dispatch loop aborts, rather than leaving a repo's fleet state silently incomplete.
trigger: any step of launching one repo's worker fails partway through
outcome: a partial dispatch failure always leaves an explicitly diagnosable orphaned state with a handoff, never a silently stuck or ambiguous fleet record
rationale: A fail-closed diagnostic-recording rule attached to the spawn-worker checkpoint, repeated identically at every failure branch of that checkpoint.

statement: Rolling back an interrupted dispatch is scoped precisely: a managed coordinator pane this exact invocation created is killed on failure, but a coordinator pane the invocation merely selected (already existing) is never touched, and once every repo has been dispatched successfully the rollback trap is disarmed so a later, unrelated failure can never retroactively kill a now-owned coordinator pane.
trigger: a dispatch using a managed coordinator pane fails partway through, or completes
outcome: rollback never destroys a coordinator pane the dispatch did not itself create, and never fires after the dispatch has genuinely succeeded
notes: tmux-pane-specific mechanism obsolete under the daemon's own process/session ownership model; the precise-scope-of-rollback discipline is a durable design lesson.
rationale: Coordinator-pane creation/rollback is tmux-specific machinery the daemon's own client/API model (clients hold no state, per CLAUDE.md) has no equivalent for; the underlying 'only roll back exactly what you created' discipline is worth preserving.

statement: A tracked-work task per targeted repo is created before dispatch commits to any worker launch when no explicit task reference was supplied, but the admission (drain) lock is held only through that first side effect and released immediately afterward, so dispatch does not hold a fleet-wide lock across the much longer per-repo worktree/launch sequence.
trigger: a dispatch is committing its first durable side effect
outcome: a concurrent drain can never race a dispatch's admission decision, while dispatch still does not hold a shared lock for its entire (much longer) execution
rationale: A precise locking-scope rule attached to the admission-check checkpoint (which is itself the drain-admission-control workflow's checkpoint, captured under bin/_sgt-drain.sh).

statement: Launching the shipping-gate validator is a bounded, gated procedure: a coordinator-owned validation run requires a worker-published readiness marker proving the exact reviewed commit and every review axis passed, an isolated validation code snapshot preserving that exact commit, and either the original dispatching coordinator or an explicitly-claimed replacement to own it — with every precondition checked before any state is committed.
trigger: a worker's code is ready for final shipping-gate validation
outcome: a validation run is only ever launched against exactly the reviewed commit, owned by exactly one accountable coordinator, with an isolated snapshot proving nothing changed underneath it
notes: Named directly in the N1 contract's Method section as the no-mistakes stress case.
rationale: Bounded, independently invocable procedure (launch validation for exactly one task/repo) with a clear completion condition and its own release/claim sub-lifecycle — matches §6.2, and is the top-level workflow that stage-context units below attach to.
alternatives_considered: stage of a larger validate-and-ship workflow

statement: A validation run can only be launched once the worker has published a readiness marker asserting the exact intent revision, the exact reviewed head commit, and that all three independent review axes (standards, spec, readiness) explicitly passed — a stale head, a mismatched intent revision, or any axis not equal to 'passed' each refuse the launch with its own specific reason.
trigger: the coordinator attempts to launch validation
outcome: validation can never be launched against work that has not been reviewed, or against a different commit than the one that was reviewed
rationale: A durable, meaningful checkpoint (has this exact commit passed every required review before validation may even start?) whose semantics survive reimplementation — matches §6.3 directly.

statement: Ownership of a task's validation launch can be transferred to a new coordinator pane only when the process claiming it can prove, by walking its own OS parent-process chain, that it genuinely runs inside the claiming pane — a caller that merely sets an environment variable claiming to be that pane cannot satisfy this and is refused.
trigger: a coordinator pane other than the original dispatching one attempts to claim validation ownership
outcome: ownership handover can never be spoofed by a process that merely claims a pane identity through an environment variable
rationale: Process-tree walking to verify pane ownership is tmux-coordinator-specific machinery; the daemon's own loopback API + bearer-token authentication (CLAUDE.md's client model) replaces the need for a process-identity proof entirely, since there is no shared interactive pane to hand over ownership of. The underlying 'never trust a self-asserted identity claim' lesson is durable.

statement: A validation launch's every state transition is written through one shared owned-write helper that stages the value to a private candidate file, verifies its filesystem identity did not change between staging and publishing, publishes it via a hard-link rename, and records the exact path as owned — so every one of dozens of state files in a validation run shares one crash-safe, ownership-verified write path rather than each writing ad hoc.
trigger: any of a validation launch's many durable facts is written
outcome: every validation state write is crash-safe and independently verifiable as owned by this exact invocation, uniformly across the whole procedure
rationale: A single write primitive reused dozens of times across the validation-launch procedure (window name, stage, pane, snapshot identity, intent transport, release handshake, etc.) — the canonical §6.6 shared-helper.

statement: Validation runs against a code-cloned isolated snapshot, not the worker's live worktree — created via a shared, no-checkout local clone then checked out at the exact reviewed commit, with an owner marker recorded inside the clone's own git directory — so a shipping-gate run can never observe a worktree the worker continues to mutate concurrently.
trigger: a validation run needs a code snapshot to validate against
outcome: a shipping-gate run's verdict is always about a genuinely frozen snapshot of exactly the reviewed commit, never a moving worktree
notes: Directly analogous to sergeant-rs's own git-worktree-per-stage isolation invariant (proposal §3.6/§6.7 'Git work surfaces are host-native').
rationale: A durable checkpoint (does validation run against a genuinely isolated, frozen snapshot of the reviewed commit?) that matters under any implementation — matches §6.3.

statement: Whether a validation run's canonical intent is passed to the shipping-gate tool via a private file path or via argv is decided once, probed against the actually-installed build's real capability (not assumed), and requires explicit operator consent to select the argv transport at all, because argv exposes intent content through process listings and /proc.
trigger: a validation launch is about to decide how to pass canonical intent
outcome: intent content is never exposed via argv without the operator's explicit, per-run consent, and the transport decision is grounded in what the installed tool actually supports
rationale: A consent/privacy rule enforced at the validation-launch checkpoint, echoing the same principle already captured as an agents-invariant in bin/_sgt-intent.sh; here it is the concrete enforcement point, not the standing rule itself.

statement: Cleanup of a completed task is a bounded procedure that removes every repo's worktree (returning a treehouse lease or removing a plain git worktree) and, only when every repo is being cleaned at once, retires the fleet state directory itself — refusing to run at all unless every targeted repo's status is safely terminal, requiring the owning tracked-work task to be closed as well.
trigger: a task's repos have all reached a safely terminal state and the operator wants to reclaim resources
outcome: worktrees are reclaimed and fleet state is retired only when every safety precondition (terminal status, closed tracked-work, response-handshake completeness) holds
rationale: Bounded, independently invocable procedure with a rich completion condition (every repo safely terminal, tracked work closed) — matches §6.2, and is the top-level workflow every stage-context/stage unit below attaches to.

statement: Cleanup refuses to remove a worktree unless the owning tracked-work task is verifiably closed — and it distinguishes 'not closed yet' from 'could not even be looked up', reporting the infrastructural failure by itself rather than letting an unreadable task tracker silently masquerade as 'not terminal'.
trigger: cleanup is checking whether a repo's tracked work is done before removing its worktree
outcome: a diagnosability failure (couldn't check) is never confused with a real safety refusal (checked, and it's not closed)
rationale: A diagnosability rule attached to the terminal-precondition checkpoint, echoing the same distinct-exit-code-per-failure-cause discipline seen in sgt-owning_td_task_state's sibling checks throughout this partition.

statement: Cleanup never trusts a fleet-recorded worktree path as sufficient proof of ownership on its own; the resolved owning repository must be the exact same repository a previous pass recorded (verified by a repo identity, not just a path), and any recorded worktree that is present must independently be verified to belong to that owning repository, because a worktree replaced by an unrelated repository would otherwise answer lookups out of a foreign tracked-work database.
trigger: cleanup needs to resolve which repository owns a fleet repo's tracked work
outcome: tracked-work status can never be looked up against the wrong repository just because a path happens to coincide
rationale: A fail-closed identity-verification rule attached to the terminal-precondition checkpoint's resolution logic.

statement: Before any process is signalled for termination, cleanup verifies a recorded PID's actual start time still matches the recorded start time to rule out PID reuse; when the recorded PID is gone but live processes remain in its process group, cleanup only proceeds if the worker was its own process-group leader, and otherwise refuses outright with a fail-closed diagnostic rather than guessing which processes are safe to kill.
trigger: cleanup needs to terminate an escaped or still-live worker process
outcome: cleanup can never kill an unrelated process that has inherited a recycled PID or PGID
notes: Same PID/start-time verification pattern independently restated across sgt-drain-force, sgt-recover, and here — a recurring, shared safety property of this codebase's process-termination code, not a one-off.
rationale: Deterministic identity-verification machinery reused across every process-termination path in this partition (drain-force, recover, cleanup all restate this same check) — matches §6.6.

statement: Cleanup preserves and can replay every field of a consumed response's evidence — including the worker's own post-application proof — before retiring fleet state, and it refuses to retire fleet state at all while an unfinishable response is still outstanding, so retiring a task can never silently discard evidence that a delivered instruction was never actually consumed.
trigger: fleet state for a task is about to be retired
outcome: retiring a task never destroys evidence of a response that was delivered but never proven consumed
rationale: The exact same four-field response-archive shape defined once in bin/_sgt-response-lock.sh is consumed and validated here — the same shared-context contract restated at its consuming checkpoint, so this unit documents the consumer side of that shared shape.

statement: Removing a worktree publishes a durable, resumable cleanup-phase record before the removal begins and updates it again once removal completes, so that a cleanup interrupted mid-removal can be safely retried later: the retry re-verifies exact identity of every recorded fact (owner repo, worker evidence, worktree Git identity) rather than assuming the prior attempt's state is still accurate.
trigger: cleanup is retried after a prior invocation was interrupted mid-worktree-removal
outcome: a retried cleanup can always resume exactly where an interrupted attempt left off, without either repeating destructive work unsafely or losing track of what already happened
rationale: A durable checkpoint (has this worktree's removal actually completed, and can a retry prove that?) whose crash-safety semantics matter under any implementation — matches §6.3.

statement: Cleanup only ever retires the whole fleet-state directory for a task when every repo is being cleaned together (no repo filter given); a single-repo-scoped cleanup invocation only ever removes that one repo's worktree and never touches the shared task-level fleet state.
trigger: cleanup is invoked, optionally scoped to a single repo
outcome: a task's shared fleet-level state (brief, intent, notifications) is only ever retired once every one of its repos has actually been cleaned up
rationale: A scoping rule that governs when the retire-fleet-state checkpoint is even reached, not a checkpoint by itself.

statement: Cleanup is only ever permitted to run when the worker's process cwd is verifiably not still inside the worktree being removed — verified via a system-wide process-working-directory scan (lsof) immediately before removal — so a worktree is never deleted while some process, tracked or untracked, still has it open.
scope: worker termination safety / worktree removal precondition
trigger: a worktree is about to be removed
outcome: a worktree removal can never proceed while any process — even one cleanup itself never launched or tracks — is still using it as its working directory
rationale: A fail-closed precondition attached to the remove-worktree checkpoint, independent of and broader than the recorded-process-tree termination logic (it catches processes cleanup never even knew about).
